# Cogeneration and On-Site Power {#sec-cogen}

## Cogeneration

Cogeneration, also called combined heat and power (CHP), generates useful heat and electricity (or shaft power) in one integrated system. A CHP system pairs a prime mover (a steam turbine, gas turbine, reciprocating engine, microturbine, or fuel cell) with a generator, heat recovery, and an electrical connection, and takes its name from the prime mover [@epa-2007]. The prime mover can burn biomass, biogas, natural gas, or coal, and its recovered heat can raise steam, heat water or air for drying, or drive absorption chillers.

Canadian industry already runs biomass CHP in the pulp and paper, chemical, wood products, and food processing industries. A typical plant fires a biomass boiler whose steam drives a back-pressure or extraction turbine, with the exhaust or extracted steam serving the process; using the heat this way can raise overall efficiency by more than 35 % [@epa-2007].

### How CIMS represents cogeneration

CIMS does not treat cogeneration as a service of its own. A CHP unit is one of the technologies competing to supply a sector's **Steam** node (see @sec-industrial-heat): the heat is the service it provides, and the electricity is a co-product that offsets the site's purchased power. This puts CHP in direct competition with boilers, heat pumps, and the other heat-supply technologies on the full lifecycle cost of meeting the steam demand.

The CHP technologies at the Steam nodes are:

- **Gas-turbine CHP**, simple or combined cycle, where the turbine exhaust raises process steam in a heat-recovery steam generator;
- **Reciprocating engine CHP**;
- **Back-pressure or extraction steam-turbine CHP**, typically behind a fuel-fired or biomass boiler;
- **Fuel-cell CHP**;
- **Biomass gasifier CHP**; and
- **Gas-turbine or engine CHP with post-combustion capture**.

Their descriptions, types, and readiness levels are in the Steam technology list in @sec-industrial-heat.

## On-site power generation

Some sites generate electricity with no useful heat recovered: diesel and gas generator sets at off-grid mines and oil-and-gas sites, gas turbines and engines, condensing steam turbines, power plants burning by-product gases, and solar, wind, and storage in site microgrids. At isolated northern mines, diesel can supply more than 80 % of site energy. The boundary with cogeneration is heat recovery: a unit that supplies useful heat competes at the Steam node, and one that does not competes for on-site power.

The hierarchy carries an **On-Site Power** node in the Mining sector only. Waste-heat power and other power-only options could serve other sectors (cement, iron and steel, glass, refining, chemicals, pulp and paper, metal smelting, and offshore oil platforms), but those sectors have no on-site power node yet.
